note: D3 adds one thing to the infrastructure - a scheduling mechanism - and the choice between host cron and in-process is the human's, so this stage designs for both and picks neither. The OK rows are the ones infrastructure, monitoring or the pipeline genuinely carries. The large N/A set is deliberate: most of D3's 113 upstream NFRx.y are application-level - money representation, ledger integrity, query shapes, error classes, authorization - and marking them OK against an infrastructure document would be a decorative mapping. Three OK rows are honest about carrying a NEGATIVE result rather than a provisioned resource: NFR25.9 is OK because monitoring-design S2 records that nothing reads log.critical and gives costed options, NFR25.12 because its alert routes to a backup step that does not exist, and NFR26.4/NFR26.5 because the design records them as a test and a constraint specifically so they are not re-invented as dashboards. NFR19.27 and NFR19.28 are OK as tracked-and-assigned rather than built: both are inherited gaps that escalate at D3 and are named with owners and a computed cost in specification S7. Findings this stage adds beyond the requirement set: the fifth table (job_heartbeat) that no requirement names and the existing governance test will fail on; the budget guard's USD 50.20 literal that matches no configuration the code produces; and the disagreement between the enable_rds default and the example file.
